name: Union Bay Natural Area (Montlake Fill)
pass: Free. Street parking or UW parking (fee on weekdays).

effort.terrain: Gravel paths, level the whole way

bestTime: Early morning, any season. Shorebird viewing is best late summer when water levels drop.
snippet: Seattle's most-birded patch, a restored landfill on Lake Washington next to the UW campus with over 260 species recorded. Ponds, marsh, and meadow are packed into a flat, easy loop, and something is always happening: rails muttering in the cattails, eagles working the bay, and a steady parade of local birders happy to share what's around. Reachable by light rail.

spring.note: Songbird migration and nesting waterfowl; swallows swarm the ponds.

summer.note: Broods of ducklings on the ponds; watch for Green Herons at dawn.

fall.note: Mudflat edges pull in shorebirds; sparrows move through the meadows.

winter.note: Big waterfowl numbers on the bay and ponds.

sources.title: UW Botanic Gardens: Union Bay Natural Area
WTA: Bird Watching Hikes in Washington

name: Discovery Park
pass: Free. Limited beach-lot passes available at the visitor center.

effort.distance: 2.8 mile loop; add about 1.5 miles round trip to West Point beach
effort.gain: About 300 ft if you drop to the beach
effort.terrain: Well-kept dirt and paved trails; the climb back from the beach is a real hill

bestTime: Morning for forest and meadow birds; any daylight hour works for seawatching at West Point, and winter is prime for it.
snippet: Seattle's largest park, 534 acres of forest, open bluff meadows, and a lighthouse point jutting into Puget Sound, with nearly 300 species on the list. You can bird three habitats in one walk: chickadee and creeper flocks in the woods, raptors and sparrows on the bluffs, and loons, grebes, and sea ducks off West Point. It feels far wilder than a city park has any right to.

spring.note: Migrants drop into the forest edges; terns return to the Sound.

summer.note: Guillemots and auklets fish off West Point; martins use the snags.

fall.note: Seawatching picks up; sparrows flood the meadows.

winter.note: The best season at West Point: loons, grebes, and sea ducks close to shore.

name: Seward Park

effort.gain: Flat on the paved loop; interior forest trails climb gently
effort.terrain: Paved, stroller-friendly shoreline path; soft dirt trails through the forest

bestTime: Early morning for forest birds; dusk in late summer for Barred Owls. Winter mornings for lake waterfowl.
snippet: A peninsula of genuine old-growth forest sticking into Lake Washington, home to some of the biggest trees left in Seattle. This is the place for forest birds: Barred Owls are seen regularly, Pileated Woodpeckers drum from the big firs, and Bald Eagles nest here every year. The flat paved loop around the shoreline makes it one of the most relaxed birding walks in the city, and the Seward Park Audubon Center runs regular guided walks.

spring.note: Eagles on the nest; dawn chorus in the old growth is superb.

summer.note: Listen for young Barred Owls begging at dusk.

fall.note: Thrushes and kinglets move back down into the lowland forest.

winter.note: Rafts of divers off the point; quiet forest full of mixed flocks.

sources.title: Greater Seattle on the Cheap: Bird watching in the Puget Sound region

name: Magnuson Park

effort.distance: 1 to 3 miles of flat wandering, your choice
effort.terrain: Wide gravel and paved paths through the wetland complex

bestTime: Morning; the wetland ponds are liveliest early. Winter brings the most waterfowl variety.
snippet: A former naval air station reborn as a chain of wetland ponds and meadows along Lake Washington, now one of north Seattle's richest bird spots with about 225 species recorded. The pond loop delivers close views of teal, herons, and marsh wrens, the meadows hold sparrows and raptors, and the swimming-beach shoreline turns up loons and grebes in winter. Easy, flat, and great for a quick session.

spring.note: The ponds fill with nesting activity; rails call from the reeds.

summer.note: Buntings have summered in the meadows; goldfinches everywhere.

fall.note: Sparrow flocks build; Merlins hunt the meadows.

winter.note: Scan the lake from the beach; ducks pack the ponds.

name: Juanita Bay Park

effort.distance: Under 1 mile of boardwalks and paved path
effort.terrain: Boardwalks and paved causeway; fully accessible

bestTime: Morning light is beautiful on the bay; good at any hour. Eastside Audubon leads regular walks here.
snippet: Kirkland's wetland showpiece: boardwalks reach out over a lily-pad bay on Lake Washington where Wood Ducks, herons, and turtles go about their business at close range. It may be the best spot in the region for effortless, close-up wetland birding, which is why Eastside Audubon uses it for interpretive walks and evening bird outings. Bring binoculars, but honestly you barely need them.

spring.note: Wood Ducks pair up; the marsh is loud with wrens.

summer.note: Grebe and duck broods weave through the lily pads.

winter.note: Hundreds of waterfowl in the bay; eagles perch in the cottonwoods.

name: Marymoor Park
habitat: River slough, wet meadow, cottonwood forest
pass: County parking fee (pay station), currently a few dollars per day.

effort.distance: Bird Loop is about 2 miles; up to 4 miles of flat trails
effort.terrain: Gravel paths and boardwalk along the Sammamish Slough

bestTime: Early morning before the park gets busy. A weekly bird survey has run here for decades, and Eastside Audubon hosts events regularly.
snippet: Redmond's giant county park hides a first-rate birding circuit along the Sammamish Slough: wet meadows, cottonwood groves, and a marsh boardwalk with about 250 species recorded. Ospreys nest on the light towers, eagles patrol the river, and the meadows are one of the most reliable places on the Eastside for savannah sparrows and, in summer, Lazuli Buntings. The long-running weekly survey means the bird life here is exceptionally well documented.

spring.note: Ospreys return to the nest platforms; the slough edges sing.

summer.note: Check the meadow snags for buntings and kestrels.

fall.note: Sparrow numbers surge along the Bird Loop.

winter.note: Open meadows attract shrikes and raptors.

sources.title: WTA: Bird Watching Hikes in Washington

name: Edmonds Waterfront & Marsh
pass: Free street and lot parking near the ferry terminal.

effort.distance: 1 to 2 miles of flat strolling between the pier, beach, and marsh viewpoints
effort.terrain: Sidewalks, pier decking, and viewing platforms; fully accessible

bestTime: Fall through spring is prime. The fishing pier is good at any tide; check the marsh at high tide.
snippet: The easiest saltwater birding in the region: a public fishing pier that puts you directly over the water, with grebes, loons, and sea ducks often just yards away. Steps from the pier, Edmonds Marsh is one of the last urban saltmarshes on Puget Sound, with viewing platforms over the pickleweed. Between the two you can tally a serious list without ever really leaving town, and the ferry dock adds a bonus scan of the shipping lanes.

spring.note: Brant linger into spring; martins arrive at the nest boxes.

summer.note: Quietest season on the water, liveliest at the marsh.

fall.note: Seabird numbers build fast from September.

winter.note: Peak season: the pier can be spectacular on calm winter mornings.

name: Billy Frank Jr. Nisqually NWR
habitat: River delta, estuary, freshwater marsh, riparian forest
pass: $3 per vehicle daily fee (federal passes accepted).

effort.distance: Twin Barns loop 1 mile; estuary boardwalk extends the walk to about 4 miles round trip
effort.terrain: Boardwalks and gravel dikes the entire way; largely accessible
effort.rating: Easy, but the full boardwalk is a long flat walk

bestTime: Winter and migration are outstanding. Aim for a rising or high tide, which pushes birds close to the boardwalk. The last mile of boardwalk closes seasonally for hunting season, roughly October through January, so check refuge conditions.
snippet: The premier birding destination in the South Sound: a restored river delta where the Nisqually meets saltwater, walked entirely on boardwalks and dikes. In winter the estuary hosts thousands of waterfowl, clouds of Dunlin twist over the flats with Peregrines in pursuit, and the riparian loop is thick with songbirds. With over 270 species recorded, a good day here can top 60 species without hurrying. Named for the Nisqually tribal leader who fought for the treaty fishing rights upheld in the Boldt decision.

spring.note: Shorebird migration peaks late April to early May on the flats.

summer.note: Quieter, but the riparian forest stays busy with breeders.

fall.note: Waterfowl and raptors pour back in through October.

winter.note: Peak spectacle: tens of thousands of ducks and geese on the delta.

sources.title: USFWS: Billy Frank Jr. Nisqually NWR

name: Crockett Lake (Whidbey Island)
habitat: Shallow brackish lagoon, wet pasture, beach
pass: Free roadside viewing; Discover Pass needed if you park at adjacent Fort Casey State Park.

effort.distance: Roadside pullouts and short walks; as little or as much as you like
effort.terrain: Viewing is mostly from road shoulders and pullouts along Highway 20; a scope helps

bestTime: July through September for shorebirds; winter for raptors. Combine with the Coupeville ferry ride and Fort Casey.
snippet: A shallow lagoon beside the Coupeville ferry landing that is, acre for acre, the best shorebird spot in the Puget Sound region. In late summer the muddy edges swarm with sandpipers, plovers, and dowitchers, with falcons and harriers never far behind. It is drive-up birding: pull off the highway, set up a scope, and let the birds come to you. In winter the wet fields hold Short-eared Owls and rough legs of raptors working the grass.

summer.note: Fall shorebird migration starts by early July and is the main event.

winter.note: Raptor central; dusk owl-watching over the fields.

name: Fort Ebey State Park (Whidbey Island)

effort.distance: 2 to 5 miles depending on route; 25 miles of trails in the park
effort.gain: Rolling, up to a few hundred feet
effort.terrain: Forest singletrack and bluff trails; some ups and downs

bestTime: Morning for forest birds; the bluff is a fine afternoon seawatch. WTA highlights the Old Gun Battery Trail for nesting owls.
snippet: A former coastal defense fort on Whidbey's west side where dense forest meets a high bluff over the Strait of Juan de Fuca. The draw is variety with a view: owls and woodpeckers in the woods, kinglet and chickadee flocks along the trails, and from the bluff a raptor's-eye seawatch over kelp beds where scoters, loons, and auklets ride the tide rips. Combine it with Crockett Lake for a full Whidbey day.

spring.note: Owlets fledge near the gun battery; forest song peaks.

summer.note: Auklets feed in the rips below the bluff.

fall.note: Seabirds stream past; thrushes return to the understory.

name: Dungeness National Wildlife Refuge
habitat: Sand spit, saltwater, bluff forest, lagoon
pass: $3 per family daily fee (federal passes accepted).

effort.distance: Forest bluff loop under 1 mile; the spit is up to 11 miles round trip to the lighthouse
effort.gain: About 130 ft down to the spit and back up
effort.terrain: Easy forest trail, then soft sand and cobble on the spit; walking the spit is a genuine workout
effort.rating: Easy to strenuous, entirely up to you

bestTime: Fall through spring for waterbirds. Walk the spit on a falling tide for firmer sand. Parts of the refuge close seasonally to protect wildlife.
snippet: The longest natural sand spit in the country, curling five miles into the Strait of Juan de Fuca with a lagoon on one side and open water on the other. Even the short bluff trail delivers: Harlequin Ducks and Brant work the shallows, seabirds stream past offshore, and the protected lagoon shelters huge waterfowl rafts. Walking to the lighthouse is a full-day pilgrimage; birding just the first mile of spit is nearly as good. About 90 minutes from Seattle via the Edmonds ferry, and worth every one of them.

spring.note: Brant stage in the bay before flying north.

summer.note: Quieter, with nesting seabirds offshore; check refuge closures.

fall.note: Shorebirds on the spit tip; loons move south offshore.

winter.note: Peak waterbird season; the lagoon is packed.
